items.abstract: <jats:p>Building agentic systems around frozen foundation models remains largely a craft: chains of thought, reflection loops, tool calls, and multi-agent topologies are assembled by hand. Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) recasts that craft as a search problem. In this paper we survey the ADAS literature from 2022 to 2026 through a unifying four-axis framework that re-casts the three classical pillars of neural architecture search (NAS) in an agentic setting: the optimization target (the prompt, the parameters of a compound system, the workflow topology, a modular cell, or full code), the search strategy (LLM-as-optimizer, textual gradients, evolutionary and quality-diversity search, MCTS, Bayesian or surrogate methods, and RL/DPO), the representation (a natural-language string, a modular DSL, a graph, or code), and the feedback signal (a scalar, a preference, a natural-language critique, a surrogate, or novelty). We classify thirty-three methods along these axes, spanning 2022 to 2026 and including the recent surge of 2026 work, trace two structural tensions—expressiveness versus searchability and feedback richness versus credit assignment—and examine evaluation practice, including cost, transfer, contamination, and reward hacking. We conclude with the safety problems that recursive self-improvement makes concrete and the open directions they impose.</jats:p>
title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems: A Survey of Algorithms for Searching, Optimizing, and Evolving LLM Agents, Workflows, and Prompts
Architectural Design Patterns for Agentic Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-agentic AI systems (MAS) amplify capability by distributing work across specialized, semi-autonomous agents, but they also expand the attack surface with greater tools, more boundaries, more inter-agent communications, and more chances for emergent behaviors to go wrong. As we highlight in this document, security by design for MAS will require intertwining governance and compliance aligned to AI risk frameworks (NIST AI RMF) and evolving standards and regulations (ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act), secure architectures with strong isolation (sandboxing) and least privilege enforcements, MAS-specific threat modeling, pre-deployment and continuous security testing that includes red teaming of inter-Agent channels, and runtime monitoring and response. Moreover, security must be embedded at every stage of Agent development, governance, and execution.</jats:p>
title: Security-by-Design for Multi-Agentic AI Systems
Towards Multi-Agentic AI for automated software design and modelling: challenges and opportunities

items.abstract: <jats:p>The financial services industry is undergoing a paradigm shift as artificial intelligence evolves from passive automation to active agency. Agentic AI systems-comprising autonomous, adaptive, and collaborative AI agents-are emerging as transformative tools capable of planning, executing, and optimizing complex financial workflows with minimal human oversight. This paper explores the application of agentic AI systems across three critical domains: regulatory compliance, auditing, and financial modeling. In compliance and auditing, multi-agent architectures demonstrate significant potential for automating regulatory workflows through specialized agents that parse regulations, monitor transactions, generate transparent audit trails, and perform model risk management tasks. Research indicates that agentic systems can achieve pre-deployment compliance detection rates of 89% compared to 43% for conventional testing methods, with segregation-of-duties enforcement efficacy reaching 96%. These systems leverage large language models and multi-agent collaboration to execute tasks such as checking compliance documentation, model replication, conceptual soundness verification, and outcome analysis. In financial modeling, agentic AI systems automate data ingestion, scenario analysis, and model maintenance while reducing human error and accelerating workflows that previously required days or weeks of manual effort. Multiagent frameworks coordinate specialized agents for signal discovery, code generation, and backtesting, enabling self-improving research cycles in quantitative finance. The integration of agentic AI with traditional software infrastructure is complementary rather than disruptiveagents operate atop existing systems, navigating and activating software to fetch data, trigger analytical engines, and orchestrate end-to-end processes while maintaining auditability and traceability. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain, including model drift, interpretability concerns, regulatory uncertainties, governance requirements, and the need for robust oversight frameworks to ensure transparent and responsible AI deployment in highstakes financial environments. This paper synthesizes current research, examines architectural approaches, evaluates practical applications, and delineates key challenges and future research directions for agentic AI in financial services.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI Systems for Automated Financial Services: A New Paradigm for Compliance, Auditing, and Financial Modeling
